note: Q62 makes DA committee rotation retroactive. The defect had two sites, verified against source before the change rather than taken from the execution plan's line anchors, which had drifted. Site 1: `ApplyToStateQueue` read no DA params at all — the constructor carried no reference-input index for them — and decided quorum purely from the attestation datum's own frozen `da_threshold`, so a quorum gathered under a committee governance had since replaced stayed applicable forever. Site 2: `get_da_params` decoded `DaParamsDatum` and trusted its `committee_signers_hash` without ever recomputing `blake2b_256(committee)`, so a forged params datum carrying a rotated committee under the pre-rotation hash satisfied every comparison any consumer made against that field. The fix reads the current authenticated params in the apply branch and requires the attestation's frozen `committee_signers_hash` and `da_threshold` to still equal the governed values, and re-derives the committee hash inside the single authenticated params reader. Equality of the committee hash rather than `attestation_count >= governed threshold` is deliberate and is measured: what is stale about such a quorum is whose signatures it holds, and a threshold that happens to be satisfied must not launder a rotated-out membership. Freezing a second value has a consequence this artifact records rather than leaves implicit: it creates a second way for an attestation to become unappliable, so the Q63 rescue condition had to be widened to the exact complement of this gate — either frozen value differing, not just the committee hash. An adversarial review of the uncommitted diff caught that; the first draft inverted only the committee half, which would have made a threshold-only governance update lock an attestation's ADA permanently. The `strandedness-completeness` group is that defect's regression test. Every count below is recomputed by the gate from an executed runner report or from the validator source; nothing here is a declaration count.

It never called `get_da_params`, and the `ApplyToStateQueue` constructor in `onchain/aiken/lib/midgard/da-attestation-types.ak` declared no `da_params_ref_input_index`, so the handler had no way to reach the governed committee even in principle.

compiler.rule: Aiken test execution for this goal is fork-only: the stock v1.1.22 build that is the authority for compilation and applied validator hashes ships a codegen defect and takes hours over this tree, so it is used only for `aiken check --skip-tests`. The gate resolves the compiler from `MIDGARD_AIKEN_BIN` then `MIDGARD_FORK_AIKEN_BIN` (CI pins only the latter) and fails closed with ERR_AIKEN_BINARY_UNPINNED when neither is set, rather than falling through to whatever `aiken` is first on PATH. Whichever resolves must then report an `aiken v1.1.23` version or the run fails closed with ERR_AIKEN_COMPILER_MISMATCH. Both behaviours are seeded self-tests, not assurances: the gate spawns itself with the variables stripped, and again against a stub binary reporting a v1.1.22 version.

groups.claim: An attestation whose frozen committee and threshold still equal the governed values applies, so the rotation rejections are not a handler that rejects everything.
groups.languageRationale: On-chain only by construction, and declared so. The claim is that a Plutus minting policy accepts a transaction, which is settled by running the handler; a Node verifier can execute no Plutus. The control runs the real `da_attestation.mint` handler end to end, including the state-queue linked-list attachment — this is the first Aiken coverage that path has ever had, so the control also establishes that the attachment fixture is genuinely valid and the five negatives below therefore fail on the governed-params comparison rather than on a malformed transaction.

groups.claim: Rotation, a governed threshold change, a forged committee hash, a stale params reference input, and an old-committee quorum are each rejected by the apply handler.
groups.languageRationale: On-chain only, for the same reason as the control: each is a Plutus handler refusing a transaction. Four of the five are strict one-field mutations of the control's transaction, so a rejection can only be attributed to the bound it names, and each was confirmed to trap at the specific `expect` it targets rather than merely to fail. `da_attestation_apply_rejects_old_committee_quorum` is the family's one compound mutation and is declared as such rather than presented as a one-field differential: it rotates the committee *and* drops the governed threshold to 1 so the frozen count of 2 clears the new bar, because it exists to kill a specific weaker fix — re-reading the params but comparing `attestation_count >= params.da_threshold` — that every one-field negative here would still pass.

groups.claim: An attestation made unappliable by a governed threshold change over an unchanged committee is rescuable, so the apply gate and the rescue condition are exact complements and no attestation can be stranded by either.
groups.languageRationale: On-chain only, and required as its own group rather than folded into the rescue path because it is the regression test for a defect this very task introduced and an adversarial review caught. Q62 adds a second frozen value to the apply gate (`da_threshold`), and therefore a second way to become unappliable. The first draft of the rescue inverted only the committee hash, so a threshold-only governance update — which the DA-params governor explicitly permits, and which its own spend-seam control test performs — produced an attestation that could never apply (the threshold no longer matched), never be rescued (the committee hash still matched), and whose `AddSignatures` path kept accepting signatures that could never amount to anything. Its ADA was locked permanently: exactly the failure D-DA5 clause (c) exists to rule out, reintroduced by the D-DA4 fix. The cited test runs the rescue against the same attestation and the same governed params as `da_attestation_apply_rejects_governed_threshold_change`, so the pair measures the complementarity directly rather than asserting it. It also covers the quorum-reached case, which the sub-threshold rescue control does not.

groups.claim: A burn-side spend redeemer may only defer to its own mint constructor: BurnForRescue is rejected against an ApplyToStateQueue mint redeemer and BurnForStateQueue against a RescueStrandedAttestation one, while the matching binding is accepted.
groups.languageRationale: On-chain only. This group exists because of a coverage gap an adversarial review identified rather than a defect: `validate_burn_binding` discriminates with two separate guards, and while a full swap of them would have been caught by the existing controls, dropping either one alone would have left every other test in the module green. That is not academic — `ApplyToStateQueue` imposes no refund binding at all, so a `BurnForRescue` satisfied by an apply redeemer would release an attestation's value with nothing constraining where it went. Both directions are therefore pinned individually rather than as a conjunction, and each was confirmed to trap at its own guard.

groups.claim: The rescue path refuses a refund short of the attestation's value, so a permissionless rescuer cannot skim the deposit.
groups.languageRationale: On-chain only, and measured here rather than under Q63 because Q63's required-group table fixes its rescue rejection group at exactly three (theft, duplicate, replay) and this is a fourth, distinct disposition. It is cited somewhere rather than left uncited on purpose: the rescue's value binding is a live branch of the validator, and an untested branch is dormant surface regardless of which goal's gate happens to own it.

groups.claim: The off-chain redeemer encoding matches the Aiken constructor declaration order, the apply redeemer carries the governed-params reference index, and the rotation predicate agrees with the on-chain state condition on both of its disjuncts.
groups.languageRationale: Off-chain only by construction, and declared so. These are claims about what the SDK puts on the wire, which no Aiken test can observe. The pairing matters: Plutus tags a constructor by its position, so reordering a declaration silently re-points every encoded redeemer at a different branch — a change no type checker on either side would catch. The suite therefore reads the constructor order out of the Aiken source and asserts the CBOR tag each TypeScript constructor actually encodes to, making it a cross-language pin rather than a restatement of the TypeScript enum against itself.

titles: abi 1 — mint constructors keep the declared Aiken order on the wire
abi 2 — spend constructors keep the declared Aiken order on the wire
abi 3 — the apply redeemer carries the governed-params reference index
predicate 1 — an attestation matching both governed values is not stranded
predicate 2 — a rotated-out committee strands the attestation
predicate 3 — a governed threshold change strands the attestation even on an unchanged committee
